query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of lightweight high-entropy alloys to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance can be explained by the formation of a stable solid solution structure with a high mixing entropy, which enhances the strength and resistance to deformation, while the lattice strain effect induced by atomic size mismatches improves corrosion resistance and low-temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Lightweight high-entropy alloys with a composition of multiple principal elements in equal or near-equal mole ratios
generation.intervention: Controlled variation of alloy composition and processing conditions to optimize the formation of a stable solid solution structure
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance testing in extreme environments, such as aerospace and rail-transport applications
generation.structural_mediator: Stable solid solution structure with a high mixing entropy
generation.mechanism: Lattice strain effect induced by atomic size mismatches, which enhances strength and resistance to deformation, and improves corrosion resistance and low-temperature strength
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance, while maintaining low density
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with similar composition and processing conditions
generation.boundary: Limitations in alloy composition and processing conditions that prevent the formation of a stable solid solution structure
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between alloy composition, processing conditions, and the formation of a stable solid solution structure, as well as the potential trade-offs between different properties

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of lightweight high-entropy alloys with different compositions and processing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the formation of a stable solid solution structure does not correlate with improved mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance, while maintaining low density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys, also known as HEAs, are generally composed of five or more elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. These alloys are stable in a disordered solid solution state owing to a high mixing entropy [,]. Over the past twenty years, there has been an explosion of interest in a novel concept of alloy design that allows for the creation of materials with superior mechanical or physical properties. These properties include high yield strengths, ductility, and fracture toughness, in addition to superior high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance. As a result of these features, HEAs have found applications in a huge range of different fields [,,,,,,,,,,]. However, despite the application potential being high, the high density of many HEAs greatly inhibits the actual deployment of these applications. For example, the density of a CoCrFeNiMn HEA is 8.1 g/cm3, while the density of refractory high-enthalpy alloys (HEAs) is more than 10 g/cm3. Both of these HEAs have a mass density that is higher than that of steel, which has a density of 7.9 g per cubic centimeter. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained popularity in aerospace and marine applications as a result of their superior mechanical properties, which surpass those of conventional materials [,]. Conventional alloys have been beaten by HEAs, as demonstrated by extensive research conducted over the past decade. These include the capacity to maintain their structure and properties at elevated temperatures, a robust resistance to microstructural changes, high hardness, and exceptional high-temperature strength. Furthermore, HEAs demonstrate outstanding resistance to high-temperature softening, corrosion, fatigue, and wear []. In contrast to conventional alloys, HEAs are composed of five or more elements, each of which contributes 5–35% to the overall composition []. The high mixing entropy of these alloys is the consequence of the uniform mixing of various elements. This high entropy results in the formation of a variety of crystal structures, such as single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, as well as mixed structures that contain multiple phases. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), firstly proposed in 2004, have attracted extensive attention due to their outstanding mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, irradiation resistance and thermal stability [,,,,]. HEAs are generally composed of at least five kinds of elements with an atomic percentage between 5% and 35% in equal mole or near equal mole ratios [,]. Differing from conventional alloys, HEAs tend to form simple solid solution structures, such as face-centered cubic (FCC), body-centered cubic (BCC) and close-packed hexagonal (HCP), rather than intermetallic compounds or amorphous phases due to their higher mix entropy [,,,]. However, the existing HEAs also contain several intermetallic compounds, which can strengthen the mechanical properties [,].
